title: The ABCDE approach
blurb: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure: one systematic way to assess and treat any patient who becomes unwell.
question: A patient in the chair suddenly says they feel strange. They are pale, breathing quickly and slow to answer questions. The dentist asks you to help assess them. In what order do you check things, and why does that order matter?

teach.h: One method for every unwell patient
teach.body: When a patient becomes unwell you rarely know the cause straight away. The ABCDE approach, used across the NHS and taught by the Resuscitation Council UK, gives the whole team one shared order to work in, whatever the cause. You assess each step, treat any problem you find before moving on, and keep reassessing. You don't need a diagnosis to start helping. Call for help early: an ABCDE problem you can't fix means 999.

letters.sub: Is it open? Can they talk?

steps.label: Safe? Responding?
steps.sub: Check danger; speak to the patient; call for help

steps.label: A: Airway
steps.sub: Fix a blocked airway before anything else

steps.label: B: Breathing
steps.sub: Sit up if breathless; oxygen 15 L/min

steps.label: C: Circulation
steps.sub: Faint or shocked? Lie flat, raise legs

steps.label: E: Exposure
steps.sub: Look for rash or swelling; keep dignity

teach.caption: If at any point the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally, stop ABCDE and start basic life support.

teach.body: The order follows what kills fastest. A blocked airway stops oxygen reaching the lungs within minutes, so it comes first. Breathing is useless without an open airway, and circulation can only carry oxygen the lungs have taken in. That's why you treat each problem as you find it: there is no point checking blood glucose while the patient is choking. A patient who is talking normally has an open airway and is breathing, which is a quick reassurance.

teach.h: What to look for at each step
head: Step
Look for
Example action
rows: Pale, clammy, weak or fast pulse
teach.caption: Snoring, gurgling or a high-pitched noise all mean a partly blocked airway. A silent patient who is trying to breathe may have a completely blocked one.

teach.h: D for Disability: the AVPU scale

teach.caption: Capillary refill: press a fingertip for 5 seconds, release and count how long the colour takes to return.

teach.text: Don't jump to the letter that matches what you think the problem is. Even if you know the patient is diabetic, check A and B first. A drowsy patient may have a blocked airway that needs fixing before you think about glucose.

items: ABCDE: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure, always in that order.
Treat each problem as you find it, then move on; reassess regularly from A.
A talking patient has an open airway and is breathing.
D uses AVPU (Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive) and blood glucose.
Call for help early; unresponsive and not breathing normally means start BLS.

summary: You can now assess any unwell patient using ABCDE: you know what to look for at each step, why the order follows the most immediate threats to life, how to use AVPU, and that you treat problems as you find them, reassess often and switch to basic life support if the patient stops breathing normally.

A.q: A patient becomes unwell in the chair. Using the ABCDE approach, what is assessed straight after the airway?
A.why: The order is Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure, so breathing follows airway.

whyNot.0: Circulation is the third step, after breathing.

A.q: While assessing an unwell patient, you hear a gurgling noise as they breathe. Which part of ABCDE does this point to?
A.why: Gurgling suggests fluid (such as saliva, blood or vomit) in the airway, which is an A problem needing suction or repositioning.

whyNot.1: Circulation is about pulse, skin colour and capillary refill, not breathing noises.
whyNot.2: Disability is about the level of response and blood glucose.
whyNot.3: Exposure is about looking at the skin for rashes, swelling or bleeding.

A.q: A patient only opens their eyes and groans when the dentist squeezes their shoulder firmly. Where are they on the AVPU scale?
A.why: Responding only to a painful stimulus, not to voice, places the patient at P on the AVPU scale.

whyNot.0: An alert patient has eyes open and is talking without prompting.
whyNot.1: V means they respond when spoken to; this patient needed a painful stimulus.
whyNot.2: Unresponsive means no response even to pain; this patient did respond.

B.q: Why is the airway always checked before the circulation?
options: Airway checks are quicker to complete
A blocked airway kills most quickly
Circulation can only be checked by doctors
Pulse checks need the patient lying down
B.why: ABCDE follows the most immediate threats to life, and a blocked airway stops oxygen getting in within minutes.

whyNot.0: Speed of the check isn't the reason; the danger to life is.
whyNot.2: Dental team members can assess circulation, for example skin colour, pulse and capillary refill.
whyNot.3: Position isn't the reason for the order; the threat to life is.

B.q: During ABCDE you find the patient is wheezy and breathless. What should you do?
options: Move on to C and come back later
Treat it now, for example sit them up
Check their blood glucose level first
B.why: In ABCDE you treat each problem as you find it: sit a breathless patient up, give oxygen and help with their inhaler, then move on.

whyNot.0: Problems are treated when found, not left for later.
whyNot.1: Lying flat usually makes breathlessness worse; breathless patients are best sitting up.
whyNot.3: Glucose is part of D; a breathing problem must be dealt with first.

B.q: What is a normal capillary refill time in a healthy adult?
B.why: Colour should return to a pressed fingertip within 2 seconds; longer suggests poor circulation.

whyNot.1: Five seconds is how long you press, not the normal refill time.
whyNot.2: Ten seconds would be very prolonged and suggest poor circulation.
whyNot.3: Thirty seconds would be a serious sign of shock, not normal.

C.q: A patient who was being assessed with ABCDE becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally. What should happen now?
options: Continue to the D and E checks
Start basic life support at once
Give oral glucose gel by mouth
C.why: Unresponsive and not breathing normally means cardiac arrest: stop ABCDE, call 999, get the AED and start CPR.

whyNot.0: Carrying on with assessment delays CPR, which must start immediately.
whyNot.2: Waiting minutes without CPR is fatal in cardiac arrest.
whyNot.3: Nothing should be given by mouth to an unresponsive patient, and CPR is the priority.

C.q: Which finding belongs under E for Exposure?
options: A respiratory rate of 30 a minute
A raised rash on the arms and neck
C.why: Exposure means looking at the skin, with dignity, for signs such as rashes, swelling or bleeding. A raised rash could point to an allergic reaction.

whyNot.0: Capillary refill is part of C, circulation.
whyNot.1: Respiratory rate is part of B, breathing.
whyNot.2: Response level (AVPU) is part of D, disability.

C.q: What oxygen flow rate is used for a patient who needs oxygen during a medical emergency in the practice?
C.why: In a dental medical emergency, oxygen is given at 15 L/min through a mask with a reservoir.

whyNot.0: 2 L/min is a low flow, not the emergency rate.
whyNot.1: 5 L/min is too low for an emergency.
whyNot.3: 25 L/min is above the standard emergency flow rate of 15 L/min.

reteach.title: Fix the leak nearest the tap first
reteach.question: Imagine oxygen travelling from the air to the brain like water through a pipe. Where would you look for a blockage first?

blocks.body: Oxygen goes in through the airway (A), into the lungs by breathing (B), then round the body in the blood (C) to reach the brain (D). If the pipe is blocked at the airway, nothing further down can work, however good the pump is. So you start at the tap and follow the flow. E is the final look over the whole body for clues you might have missed, like a rash or swelling.

steps.label: Airway
steps.sub: The way in must be open

steps.label: Disability
steps.sub: The brain uses it: is the patient alert?

blocks.text: If you fix something, go back to A and check again. Patients change quickly, and a patient who was fine at A two minutes ago may not be now.

explain.body: Is the airway open? A patient who talks normally has an open airway. Snoring, gurgling or high-pitched noises suggest a partial blockage; silent efforts to breathe suggest a complete one. Remove any dental items, use suction and open the airway.

test.q: A patient is talking to you in full sentences. What does that tell you about their airway?
test.why: Speaking in full sentences needs air moving through an open airway.

whyNot.1: A blocked airway would stop them speaking.
whyNot.2: Suction is for fluid in the airway, which would cause gurgling.
whyNot.3: Normal speech is a reliable quick sign of an open airway.

explain.body: Look at the rate, the effort and the colour, and listen for wheeze. Sit a breathless patient up, give oxygen at 15 L/min and help with their own inhaler if they have asthma.

test.q: A patient's breathing rate is 32 breaths a minute and they look anxious. How should this be interpreted?
options: A sign of a blocked airway
test.why: A normal adult rate is about 12–20 breaths a minute, so 32 is abnormally fast and needs attention.

whyNot.0: Anxiety can raise the rate, but 32 is well outside normal and must not be dismissed.
whyNot.1: Slow would be below about 12 a minute.
whyNot.2: Rate alone doesn't show a blocked airway; noises and inability to speak do.

explain.body: Check skin colour and temperature, the pulse, and capillary refill (normal is 2 seconds or less). A pale, clammy patient with a weak pulse may be fainting or shocked: lie them flat and raise their legs if appropriate.

test.q: A patient feels faint, looks pale and has a slow pulse. Which action fits the C step?
options: Check them on the AVPU scale
test.why: Lying a fainting patient flat with legs raised helps blood return to the brain.

whyNot.0: Sitting up makes a faint worse.
whyNot.2: An inhaler treats asthma, a B problem.
whyNot.3: AVPU is part of D, assessed after C.

explain.body: D: how alert is the patient? Use AVPU and check blood glucose if you suspect a hypo. E: look at the skin for rashes, swelling or bleeding, protecting the patient's dignity and keeping them warm.

test.q: Which check belongs under D for Disability?
test.why: D covers the level of response (AVPU) and blood glucose, since a low glucose can cause drowsiness or confusion.

whyNot.0: Looking for a rash is part of E, exposure.
whyNot.1: Breathing rate is part of B.
whyNot.3: Capillary refill is part of C.
